title: Who counts as married
subtitle: Formalities, same-sex marriage and civil partnership since Steinfeld
objectives: State the formal requirements for a valid marriage under the Marriage Act 1949 and identify the consequences of failing to meet them

Explain how the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 and the Civil Partnership Act 2004 — as extended in 2019 following Steinfeld — expanded the forms of legally recognised relationship available to couples
Explain why the form of relationship a couple chooses continues to determine which legal regime applies to them, both at formation and later

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the preliminaries, formalities and capacity requirements for a valid marriage in England and Wales
Extended marriage to same-sex couples from 13 March 2014 and permitted conversion of civil partnerships into marriage
Created civil partnership as a parallel status, originally restricted to same-sex couples; extended to opposite-sex couples by the Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Steinfeld) v Secretary of State for International Development [2018] UKSC 32
leadingAuthorities.role: Held that restricting civil partnership to same-sex couples was incompatible with Art 14 ECHR read with Art 8, once the government's 'wait and evaluate' justification had expired

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Marriage, civil partnership and nullity get taught as if they were purely definitional — but exam and SQE questions routinely turn on a formality or a status question buried inside a longer problem. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know the categories — this lesson checks whether you can place a couple's relationship in the right one.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. Expect scenario questions that ask you to classify a relationship correctly, not just define the categories.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take the formalities slowly — everything else in this lesson, and the nullity lesson that follows it, assumes you can state them without prompting.

overview.hook: Two ceremonies, decades apart, can look identical to a guest — flowers, vows, a register signed — and still create entirely different bundles of legal consequences. Marriage and civil partnership are not synonyms for 'a couple committed to each other'; they are statuses created by statute, each with its own gateway in and its own vocabulary for coming out. Get the gateway wrong on an exam problem and everything downstream — financial remedies, next-of-kin status, intestacy — goes wrong with it.

parts.heading: The formalities that make a marriage
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Marriage in England and Wales is a legal status created by compliance with the Marriage Act 1949 — not by cohabitation, intention, or a ceremony alone, however sincere. Two separate things have to be right: capacity (each party must be legally eligible to marry the other) and formal validity (the ceremony itself must follow one of the routes the Act prescribes).

Formal validity starts with preliminaries. For a civil route, both parties give notice of their intended marriage to a superintendent registrar and, after a statutory waiting period (28 days as standard, extendable where the Home Office flags a sham-marriage concern), the marriage may be solemnized on the authority of a superintendent registrar's certificate. The Church of England route uses its own preliminaries — banns, a common licence, or a special licence — reflecting its unique constitutional position as the only religious body that can marry couples without a separate civil ceremony.

Capacity has its own list of requirements, and this is where the 2022 reform matters most: since the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022 came into force on 27 February 2023, nobody under 18 may marry in England and Wales — full stop. The old exception allowing 16- and 17-year-olds to marry with parental consent (or a court order) has been abolished entirely. Capacity also requires that neither party is already married or in a civil partnership, that the parties are not within the prohibited degrees of relationship set out in Sch 1 to the 1949 Act (close blood relatives, and certain relatives by marriage), and that each party is capable of understanding the nature of the ceremony and validly consenting to it.

Not every formal slip invalidates a marriage. English law distinguishes trivial procedural irregularities — which leave the marriage valid — from the more serious failures that Parliament has chosen to treat as fatal. The next lesson deals with exactly where that line falls; for now, the point to hold onto is that 'we had a ceremony' is necessary but not sufficient. A valid marriage is the sum of capacity plus compliance with a prescribed formal route.

components.citation: Marriage Act 1949, s 2 (as substituted by the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022)
components.text: A marriage solemnized between persons either of whom is under the age of 18 shall be void.
elements: Minimum age of 18 applies to both parties, with no exceptions
The former 16–17 parental-consent route has been abolished (in force 27 February 2023)
A marriage solemnized below that age is void, not merely voidable — it is treated as never having existed

components.definition: The set of legal preconditions a person must satisfy before a valid marriage can be formed: minimum age of 18, not already married or in a civil partnership, not within the prohibited degrees of relationship, and sound understanding sufficient to consent. Distinct from formal validity, which concerns the ceremony itself rather than the parties' eligibility.

interaction.prompt: A 17-year-old wants to marry with both parents' written consent. Can the marriage lawfully proceed in England and Wales?
options: No — the minimum age is 18 with no exceptions, since the change that came into force in February 2023
Yes — parental consent still permits marriage from age 16
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The 2022 Act closed the 16–17 route completely; parental consent can no longer substitute for reaching 18.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not any more. The Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022 abolished the old under-18 route with parental consent — 18 is now an absolute minimum.

parts.heading: Extending marriage: the 2013 Act
parts.voice: structural — reference-style, building the framework the rest of the module assumes
body: The Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 extended marriage in England and Wales to same-sex couples, coming into force on 13 March 2014. Mechanically, same-sex couples marry through the same preliminaries and formal routes already described — the 2013 Act did not create a parallel ceremony, it opened the existing one.

Two structural features are worth knowing precisely. First, the Act allowed existing civil partners to convert their civil partnership into a marriage, with the resulting marriage treated as having subsisted since the date the civil partnership began — a deliberate choice to avoid resetting the clock on a relationship's legal history. Second, the Act built in what is usually called the 'quadruple lock': a set of protections ensuring no religious organisation or minister can be compelled to marry a same-sex couple. Individual religious bodies (other than the Church of England and the Church in Wales) may choose to opt in and conduct same-sex marriages; the Church of England and the Church in Wales are expressly excluded from opting in under the 2013 Act itself, reflecting their distinct canon-law and establishment status.

One further point earns its place here because it resurfaces in the next lesson: the grounds on which a marriage can later be annulled were amended to fit the new category. Non-consummation, historically a ground for annulling an opposite-sex marriage, was deliberately not extended to same-sex marriages — Parliament judged that the concept did not translate coherently, given how consummation had always been defined by reference to specific opposite-sex conduct. Hold that detail; Lesson 2 builds directly on it.

components.label: The 2013 Act's key mechanics
points: Extends marriage to same-sex couples in England and Wales from 13 March 2014
Existing civil partners may convert their partnership into a marriage, backdated to the start of the civil partnership
The 'quadruple lock' protects religious bodies from compulsion; other denominations may opt in, but the Church of England and the Church in Wales cannot currently do so under the 2013 Act
Non-consummation is not a ground for annulling a same-sex marriage — contrast opposite-sex marriage, covered in Lesson 2

interaction.prompt: Put these milestones in the order they occurred.
items: Civil Partnership Act 2004 creates civil partnership, restricted to same-sex couples
Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 receives Royal Assent
Same-sex marriage becomes lawful in England and Wales (13 March 2014)
Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019 extend civil partnership to opposite-sex couples
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: civil partnership first (2004, same-sex only), then same-sex marriage (2013 Act, in force 2014), then civil partnership opened up in the other direction (2019) after Steinfeld.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — civil partnership existed for same-sex couples first; same-sex marriage followed nearly a decade later; civil partnership was only opened to opposite-sex couples after the Steinfeld litigation, in 2019.

parts.heading: Steinfeld and the extension of civil partnership
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: The Civil Partnership Act 2004 created civil partnership as a parallel status for same-sex couples, giving them nearly all the legal consequences of marriage without using the word 'marriage' — a deliberate political compromise at a time when Parliament was not yet willing to legislate for same-sex marriage itself. Once the 2013 Act arrived, same-sex couples had a genuine choice between marriage and civil partnership. Opposite-sex couples still had only one option: marriage.

Rebecca Steinfeld and Charles Keidan, a different-sex couple, wanted a civil partnership rather than a marriage — not for any technical reason, but out of principled objection to what they regarded as marriage's historically patriarchal associations. The Civil Partnership Act 2004 barred them: civil partnership was, on its face, only available to same-sex couples. They challenged that restriction as unlawful discrimination.

The Supreme Court agreed. The government had originally defended the restriction on the basis that it needed time to 'wait and evaluate' how same-sex marriage bedded in before deciding what to do about civil partnership's future — a legitimate aim, for a time. But by the point the case reached the Supreme Court, years had passed with no decision taken. The Court held that an interim policy of inaction cannot remain a proportionate justification indefinitely: once the evaluation period has plainly run its course without a decision, continuing to treat opposite-sex couples differently, with no article 8 or 14 ECHR justification left standing, becomes unlawful discrimination.

The government's response was not primary legislation but the Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019, in force from 2 December 2019, which extended civil partnership to opposite-sex couples on essentially the same terms as the same-sex regime already in place.

components.caseName: R (Steinfeld) v Secretary of State for International Development
components.factsShort: An opposite-sex couple wanted a civil partnership rather than a marriage but were barred, since civil partnership was then restricted to same-sex couples under the Civil Partnership Act 2004.
components.ratioShort: Restricting civil partnership to same-sex couples breached Art 14 ECHR (read with Art 8) once the government's 'wait and evaluate' justification for the interim inequality had expired without a decision being taken.

expanded.facts: Rebecca Steinfeld and Charles Keidan had been in a long-term relationship and wished to formalise it through a civil partnership rather than marriage, citing their opposition to what they saw as the historically patriarchal and religious connotations of marriage. Because s 1 of the Civil Partnership Act 2004 confined civil partnership to same-sex couples, the couple were unable to register one. They brought judicial review proceedings arguing that the restriction was incompatible with their Convention rights.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court held that the difference in treatment fell within the ambit of Article 8 (private and family life) and amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation contrary to Article 14. The government's stated justification — that it needed time to assess the impact of extending marriage to same-sex couples before deciding civil partnership's future — was capable of justifying a temporary inequality, but could not justify an indefinite one. By the time of the hearing, the evaluation period had plainly elapsed with no decision made, so the continuing restriction could no longer be justified.
expanded.significance: Steinfeld did not itself rewrite the Civil Partnership Act; it declared the existing restriction incompatible with the Convention and left it to government to remedy. The remedy came via secondary legislation — the Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019 — rather than a fresh Act of Parliament, illustrating how a declaration of incompatibility under the Human Rights Act can trigger swift executive action without full primary legislation.

parts.heading: Why the chosen form still matters
parts.voice: direct — sets up the trap the tests will probe
body: By 2019, marriage and civil partnership had converged so far in substance that it is tempting to treat them as fully interchangeable. Resist that temptation — it is the single most common trap in this area of the syllabus. The two statuses remain distinct in their entry ceremony, in the vocabulary used to end them, and in a handful of surviving quirks that examiners like to test precisely because students assume they no longer exist.

The clearest surviving distinction is terminology on the way out: a marriage ends in divorce; a civil partnership ends in dissolution. Lesson 3 shows that the modern no-fault statutory scheme is now essentially identical in substance for both — but a problem question that uses the word 'dissolution' is telling you, deliberately, that the parties are civil partners, and a script that talks about 'divorcing' civil partners has already gone wrong.

The two statuses also still differ in ceremony. Marriage has a religious solemnization route (subject to the quadruple lock); civil partnership formation has historically been a civil, non-religious act of signing a document, though reforms since 2019 allow couples to add belief-based content to the civil partnership ceremony if they choose — it is still not a religious marriage rite. And the underlying reasons couples choose one status over the other are not always about substance: Steinfeld itself shows a couple choosing civil partnership specifically to avoid marriage's associations, a choice the law now has to respect rather than treat as a technicality.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that, after 2019, 'marriage and civil partnership are now legally identical in every respect,' and stop analysing the scenario's terminology.
components.whyItsWrong: Convergence in substance is not the same as identity in form. The entry ceremony, the vocabulary of ending the relationship (divorce vs dissolution), and a small number of historical quirks (e.g. how the two statuses interact with older pension scheme rules predating full alignment) still differ. A problem question that specifies 'civil partners' or 'dissolution' is signalling the correct legal box — missing that signal means applying the wrong label to an otherwise correct analysis.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you this couple are civil partners rather than spouses.
interaction.scenarioText: Aisha and Ben have been together for eleven years. They registered their relationship at their local register office in a short civil ceremony with two witnesses, and last year they applied to court to bring proceedings for dissolution after separating.
tappableSpans: have been together for eleven years
registered their relationship at their local register office
a short civil ceremony with two witnesses
applied to court to bring proceedings for dissolution
interaction.correctSpan: applied to court to bring proceedings for dissolution
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. 'Dissolution' is the statutory term reserved for ending a civil partnership; a marriage ends in divorce. The register-office ceremony alone is ambiguous — both marriage and civil partnership can be formed that way.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the word that only applies to one status. A civil ceremony at a register office could describe either a marriage or a civil partnership — the word that pins it down is 'dissolution', which the statutory scheme uses only for ending a civil partnership.

parts.heading: Classifying a relationship before you analyse it
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by setting up the rest of the module
body: Everything else in this module assumes you can do one thing reliably: read a fact pattern and correctly classify the relationship in front of you before applying any substantive rule to it. Get the classification wrong — treating civil partners as spouses, or missing that a 'marriage' described in the facts might in fact be void for a formality failure — and a technically correct essay on financial remedies or children law can still fail to answer the question asked.

The decision path is short but worth internalising as a genuine first step, not a formality to skip past: identify whether there was a ceremony at all; if so, identify which statutory route it followed (civil marriage, religious marriage, or civil partnership registration); then check capacity and formal validity against the relevant Act. Only once that box is ticked does it make sense to move on to what happens if the relationship breaks down — nullity, in the next lesson, and then divorce or dissolution in Lesson 3.

components.title: Classifying a couple's legal status
components.description: A decision path for working out which statutory regime applies to a relationship described in a fact pattern.

nodes.label: Did the couple undergo a formal ceremony or registration at all?
No → they are cohabitants, not spouses or civil partners (see Lesson 7)
Yes → was it a marriage ceremony or a civil partnership registration?
Marriage ceremony → check capacity (age, prohibited degrees, no existing marriage/CP) and formal validity under the Marriage Act 1949 or Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013
Civil partnership registration → check the equivalent capacity requirements under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, as extended in 2019
Requirements met → valid marriage or civil partnership; move to substantive analysis
Requirements not met → consider whether the relationship is void or voidable (Lesson 2)

components.textAlternative: First ask whether the couple underwent any formal ceremony or registration. If not, they are cohabitants. If so, identify whether it was a marriage ceremony or a civil partnership registration, then check the relevant capacity and formal validity requirements under the appropriate Act. If those requirements are met, the relationship is a valid marriage or civil partnership and substantive analysis can proceed. If not, consider whether the relationship is void or voidable, covered in the next lesson.

interaction.prompt: Priya and Tom, an opposite-sex couple, wish to register a civil partnership rather than marry. Can they do so under the law as it currently stands?
options: Yes — since the Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019, opposite-sex couples may register a civil partnership on essentially the same terms as same-sex couples
No — civil partnership remains restricted to same-sex couples
Only if they can show a religious objection to marriage, as in Steinfeld
interaction.explanation: The 2019 Regulations removed the same-sex restriction entirely; no couple has to justify their choice the way Steinfeld and Keidan had to argue for it in litigation — the option is now simply available.

testPool.prompt: Name the two elements that must both be present for a marriage to be validly formed in England and Wales.
acceptableAnswers: capacity to marry and compliance with formalities
testPool.modelAnswer: Capacity to marry (age, no prohibited relationship, not already married or in a civil partnership, sound understanding) and formal validity (a ceremony that complies with one of the routes prescribed by the Marriage Act 1949 or the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013).

testPool.prompt: Name the Act, and its date of force, that abolished marriage under 18 with parental consent in England and Wales.
acceptableAnswers: Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022, 27 February 2023
testPool.modelAnswer: The Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022, in force from 27 February 2023, which raised the minimum marriage age to 18 with no exceptions.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a ground on which the 2013 Act's 'quadruple lock' protects religious bodies?
options: No religious organisation can be compelled to marry a same-sex couple
The Church of England and Church in Wales cannot currently opt in to conducting same-sex marriages under the 2013 Act
Other religious bodies may opt in if they choose
All religious bodies must obtain a civil partnership licence before conducting any marriage
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no such licensing requirement — it is invented. The quadruple lock is about protecting religious bodies from compulsion and setting out how non-Church-of-England/Wales bodies may opt in, not about requiring any body to hold a civil partnership licence to conduct marriages.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains why Steinfeld succeeded before the Supreme Court?
options: Because civil partnership is inherently a superior legal status to marriage
Because the government's justification for the temporary inequality had expired without a decision being taken, leaving no continuing justification under Art 14/Art 8 ECHR
Because the Civil Partnership Act 2004 was found to be entirely void
testPool.trapExplanation: The case turns on proportionality and the lapse of a time-limited justification, not on any ranking of the two statuses, and the 2004 Act was never declared void — only the same-sex restriction within it was found incompatible with Convention rights.

testPool.prompt: Under Marriage Act 1949, s 2 (as substituted in 2023), what is the legal status of a marriage where one party was 17 at the time of the ceremony, even with parental consent?
options: Void
Voidable
Valid, provided both parents consented in writing
testPool.explanation: The 2022 reform makes under-18 marriage void outright, not merely voidable, and removed the parental-consent exception entirely — there is no route to validity below 18.

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the pre-2019 and post-2019 position on civil partnership under the Civil Partnership Act 2004?
options: Before 2019, civil partnership was restricted to same-sex couples; the 2019 Regulations extended it to opposite-sex couples on essentially the same terms
Before 2019, civil partnership was restricted to opposite-sex couples; the 2019 Regulations extended it to same-sex couples
The 2019 Regulations abolished civil partnership entirely, replacing it with marriage
testPool.explanation: Civil partnership began as a same-sex-only status in 2004; the direction of the 2019 reform was to open it up to opposite-sex couples, following Steinfeld — not to abolish it or reverse the restriction the other way.

testPool.prompt: Order the events in the Steinfeld litigation and its aftermath.
items: Steinfeld and Keidan are refused a civil partnership because civil partnership is restricted to same-sex couples
The couple bring judicial review proceedings alleging incompatibility with the ECHR
The Supreme Court holds the restriction unlawfully discriminatory
The Civil Partnership (Opposite-sex Couples) Regulations 2019 extend civil partnership to opposite-sex couples

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you this couple's relationship is a marriage, not a civil partnership.
testPool.scenarioText: Marcus and Elena married in a Church of England service after banns were read on three successive Sundays. They now wish to separate and are advised about the divorce process available to them.
tappableSpans: married in a Church of England service
banns were read on three successive Sundays
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. The Church of England ceremony with banns already signals marriage, but the decisive confirmation is the vocabulary — 'divorce' is used only to end a marriage; civil partnerships end in dissolution.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The ceremony described (Church of England, banns) already points to marriage, but the clinching detail is the terminology used for ending it — 'divorce' applies only to marriage.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario describes a status the couple cannot lawfully register, on the law as it stood immediately before December 2019?
testPool.scenarioA: A same-sex couple in October 2019 wish to register a civil partnership rather than marry.
testPool.scenarioB: An opposite-sex couple in October 2019 wish to register a civil partnership rather than marry.
testPool.explanation: Before the 2019 Regulations came into force on 2 December 2019, civil partnership remained restricted to same-sex couples — an opposite-sex couple in October 2019 was in exactly Steinfeld and Keidan's position before the remedy took effect.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario correctly uses 'dissolution' rather than 'divorce'?
testPool.scenarioA: Two women who married each other in 2015 separate and apply to end their marriage.
testPool.scenarioB: Two women who registered a civil partnership in 2010 separate and apply to end their partnership.
testPool.explanation: Marriage — including same-sex marriage — ends in divorce; only ending a civil partnership is correctly described as dissolution, regardless of the sex of the parties in either case.

testPool.prompt: Can a civil partner convert their civil partnership into a marriage without a new formal ceremony?
options: Yes — the 2013 Act permits conversion, backdated to when the civil partnership began
No — they must dissolve the partnership first and then marry separately

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that non-consummation is available as a ground to annul a same-sex marriage on the same basis as an opposite-sex marriage?
sliderLabels: Definitely available on the same basis
Definitely not available on the same basis
testPool.correctPosition: not available on the same basis
testPool.explanation: Not available on the same basis. Parliament deliberately did not extend the non-consummation ground to same-sex marriages when enacting the 2013 Act, judging that the traditional definition of consummation did not translate — a detail Lesson 2 develops in full.

testPool.prompt: Jamie, aged 17, and Sam, aged 19, are married in a register office in England, with Jamie's parents present and consenting in writing. Analyse the legal status of the marriage.
factsToOrder: Jamie is 17 at the time of the ceremony
Sam is 19 at the time of the ceremony
The ceremony takes place in a register office
Jamie's parents are present and consent in writing

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Jamie and Sam's marriage is valid given Jamie's age at the time of the ceremony.
modelAnswer.rule: Marriage Act 1949, s 2 (as substituted by the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Minimum Age) Act 2022), provides that a marriage solemnized where either party is under 18 is void, with no exception for parental consent.
modelAnswer.application: Jamie was 17 at the time of the ceremony. Parental consent, however clearly given and documented, no longer provides a route to a valid marriage below 18 — that exception was abolished with effect from 27 February 2023. Sam's age is irrelevant once Jamie's is below the threshold.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The marriage is void under s 2 of the Marriage Act 1949 as amended; Jamie's age alone is fatal, regardless of parental consent.

testPool.prompt: A same-sex couple ask a Church of England vicar to marry them in their local parish church. Under the law as it currently stands, must the vicar agree?
options: No — the Church of England is excluded from opting in to conduct same-sex marriages under the 2013 Act's quadruple lock
Yes — all places of worship must marry any couple that requests it
Only if the couple can show they have no other means of marrying
testPool.explanation: The quadruple lock specifically prevents the Church of England and the Church in Wales from being compelled, and neither can currently opt in under the 2013 Act itself — a couple in that position would need to use a civil ceremony or another religious body that has opted in.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming marriage and civil partnership became fully interchangeable after 2019. They converged in substance, not in form — the entry route, the vocabulary of ending the relationship (divorce vs dissolution), and a handful of surviving quirks still distinguish them, and problem questions rely on students noticing which one the facts describe.
